'Ozempic brothers': Smallzy shares the body shaming he got on Ryan Seacrest post

"I don't think either one of us looks unhealthy."

By Nama WinstonPublished Nov 5, 2026
2 min read
Smallzy and Ryan Seacrest. Image: Instagram
Listen to audio version of this article
Sponsored by
0:00 / 2:01
Instaread

Kent Small, popular radio host on KIIS FM, has spoken out about the outrageous body shaming on one of his recent Instagram posts.

Smallzy, as he's affectionately known in Australia, mentioned that he'd shared video of a red carpet moment with American producer Ryan Seacrest, and was floored by the comments on the post.

This morning on his show, Smallzy said, "The other week when we were in Vegas, I did the interview with Ryan Seacrest.

“There's currently 4000 comments. I'm not going to pretend it didn't bother me.

"Over the course of the next three or four days, I kept getting notifications.

“I want to read some of the comments out, because this is the internet in 2026.”

Smallzy then read a number of posts, including:

“Is that a corpse?”

“Is this a UNICEF ad?”

“Why do these two look like they are dying?”

“Bring back masculine men.”

“Ozempic brothers.”

Smallzy said, “I thought I looked really good in the video!”

He also joked, “I have had my issues with being fat over the years, so keep bringing it!” 

After reading more comments, Smallzy said, "I don't think either one of us looks unhealthy.

“But I want people to know that what you think is funny, you might be trying to be clever, or even if you're intentionally being mean, there's a real human reading those comments on the other end.”

He added that he's “strong” and has a “thick skin” after a career in the public eye, but others may not.

“So just think about what you put on the internet.”

Google, Meta and TikTok fight California's under-16s rules

"Overly broad laws like this actually break the systems we've built to help kids find high-quality, age-appropriate videos."

By Nama WinstonPublished Nov 5, 2026
2 min read
Image: Instagram

Google, Meta and TikTok have filed separate lawsuits against California to stop the state from enforcing Assembly Bill 1709, a new law that limits the features social media platforms can offer children under 16. 

The companies say the law breaches US free speech protections.

What the law requires

AB 1709 bars platforms from offering underage children "psychologically exploitative features" that could lead to compulsive use, such as personal recommendations and videos sent through autoplay. It also requires platforms to delete children's accounts that have those features.

The law takes effect on 1 January 2027 unless a judge voids it or puts it on hold.

The platforms' case

In lawsuits filed on Wednesday, the three companies said the law wrongly compels them to honour California's preferred way of presenting content to children, and puts the state's judgment in place of parents'.

They argue the law violates the First Amendment of the US Constitution. They also argue it breaches Section 230 of the federal Communications Decency Act, which broadly shields online platforms from liability over user content.

Google spokesperson José Castañeda said on Thursday: "Parents are best positioned to make the right decisions for their families. Overly broad laws like this actually break the systems we've built to help kids find high-quality, age-appropriate videos."

In its lawsuit, Meta said California cannot override its editorial judgments about how to curate and display billions of posts. It also said the law leaves children free to spend unlimited time on other online platforms that offer similar services.

TikTok said protected speech "cannot be suppressed solely to protect the young from ideas or images that a legislative body thinks unsuitable".

The lawsuits were filed in federal courts in San Francisco, Los Angeles and San Jose.

State to defend the law

California Attorney General Rob Bonta enforces state law and is the only defendant named in the suits. His office said on Thursday it was reviewing the lawsuits.

"Our office is committed to defending California's commonsense laws to protect kids online," the office said.

Governor Gavin Newsom signed AB 1709 on 10 September. At the time he said children's safety should be central to any discussion about technology, and that California "will not stand by while unregulated technology puts our children at risk".

Many US states regulate children's access to social media. Countries around the world have similar restrictions, including Australia, which bans children under 16 from social media.

Prime model: Influencer Ruby Tuesday Matthews casts AI Albo in tax protest

As the influencer protests tax rates, the ATO warns creators that gifts received for content generally must be declared.

By Natasha LeePublished Oct 26, 2026
3 min read
Ruby Tuesday Matthews and Anthony Albanese

Anthony Albanese has been given an off-the-shoulder makeover. There’s a straw hat, too. Apparently, Albo's a hat man. Who knew?

The Prime Minister’s unlikely turn as a fashion muse comes courtesy of Ruby Tuesday Matthews, who has cast an AI-generated Albo in a campaign for her clothing label ROBEY. Her reasoning? If the government takes a cut of her earnings, he can at least do some unpaid modelling.

The post comes as the Australian Taxation Office (ATO) tells content creators that free products received through their content are generally taxable.

In the post, Matthews argued that the government’s share of her earnings makes Albanese a part-owner of the business.

“Considering the government takes up to 47% of what we earn. I figured @albomp aka our the Prime Minister basically owns half of ROBEY,” she wrote. “So I invited him to do a little unpaid modelling because we’ve lost our campaign budgets. Swipe to meet our newest employee.”

‘Very Vogue. Very financially sustainable’

Matthews kept the employment framing going. “He’s contributed absolutely nothing to the creative process, never packed an order, designed the collection but somehow still gets a cut. Very generous arrangement,” she wrote.

She said the brand shot its latest campaign on an iPhone, while “my partner was drinking a VB, and our three children were running an underground fight club.”

“Very Vogue. Very financially sustainable,” Matthews wrote. She added that the brand had “spent the budget on really bloody good clothes”.

The 47% figure is the top marginal income tax rate of 45% plus the 2% Medicare levy. It applies to individuals’ taxable income above $190,000.

ATO puts influencer gifts on notice

The ATO has now released new guidance reminding creators and influencers that regular money, gifts, or perks can come with tax obligations.

“If you’re gifted something because of your content, it generally needs to be declared at its market value,” the ATO said.

ATO Assistant Commissioner Anita Challen said creators being paid “whether in cash, products or experiences” are “probably in business” for tax purposes.

“Free doesn’t mean tax‑free,” Challen said. “If it’s part of how you earn, it needs to be recorded.”

According to the ATO, income from content creation includes advertising and platform payments, sponsorships and affiliate links, tips, donations, and subscriptions, and free products, services, or experiences received for promotion.

“We see creators grow audiences fast, but their record-keeping and tax understanding doesn’t always keep up,” Challen said. “That’s what we’re trying to change.”

The ATO said creators are often caught off guard by audits. These can be triggered by data matching with platforms, its lifestyle assets program, or community tip-offs. Depending on their circumstances, creators may also need to register for the goods and services tax (GST).

What the ATO has released

The tax office has released three resources:

  • An online course for content creators in its Essentials to strengthen your small business program. It covers when content creation becomes a business, what income to declare, record-keeping, and the consequences of not complying.
  • An industry guide: Are you in the business of content creation?
  • Draft Taxation Ruling TR 2026/D2, Income tax: carrying on a business by an individual. Consultation closes on 27 November 2026.

Creators running a business can claim deductions for expenses they incur while making content. Where items are also used privately, those costs must be apportioned.

“We don’t want tax to be the thing that trips creators up,” Challen said. “These new resources are about giving creators clarity and confidence so they can focus on what they do best.”
